endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Examples may include plain-language explainers and FAQs, community town halls or listening sessions, and structured curricula delivered through Patient and Family Advisory Councils (PFACs) or related councils.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: This includes providing educational resources and support materials to enhance health literacy and enable patients to understand the information generated by AI algorithms.

evidence.title: Patient trust in the use of machine learning-based clinical decision support systems in psychiatric services: A randomized survey experiment
evidence.venue: European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists
evidence.outcome: Patient trust and distrust in machine learning-based clinical decision support systems
evidence.effect: Intervention increased trust vs active control (mean difference 5%, p=0.0096) and blank control (4%, p=0.015); reduced distrust vs active (-3%, p=0.021) and blank control (-4%, p=0.022).
evidence.quote: The intervention increased trust in ML-based clinical decision support systems when compared to the active control (mean difference in trust: 5% [95% CI: 1%;9%], t = −2.60, df = 668.5, p = 0.0096) and the blank control arm (mean difference in trust: 4% [95% CI: 1%;8%], t = −2.43, df = 645.0, p = 0.015).

commentary.bottom_line: One simulated randomized trial in Denmark with 992 patients found that an explanatory intervention raised trust by 4 to 5 percentage points and lowered distrust by 3 to 4 points compared with controls. No study measured whether plain-language materials improve patients' understanding of AI use or AI-generated information in real care.

perspectives.view: The only test is a randomized trial with 992 participants, which starts as strong evidence. Certainty falls to low because the setting was simulated, the outcomes were trust and distrust rather than comprehension, and a single study cannot show consistency. The effects were small (mean differences of 3% to 5%), with p-values between 0.0096 and 0.022.

The trial ran offline, so it does not show how explainers perform when delivered through patient portals, visit summaries, or clinic staff. Uptake, reading rates, and the effort needed to keep materials current as AI tools change remain unmeasured.

The trial suggests patients who received explanations trusted AI-supported decisions slightly more and distrusted them slightly less. Trust is a different outcome from understanding, and the study did not report whether patients could explain what the AI did or knew how to reach a clinician with questions.

Both endorsements come from voluntary CHAI frameworks. One lists plain-language explainers as an example a system may use, and the other describes educational resources without setting a requirement. Neither source ties the practice to a federal or state mandate.

commentary.research_gap: Trials in live clinical settings should test whether plain-language explainers and FAQs improve patients' comprehension of AI use and AI-generated information, and should measure trust calibration, question-asking, and requests to speak with a clinician alongside trust scores.
commentary.underserved_note: The single trial enrolled Danish patients in a simulated setting and did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Whether plain-language materials work for the patients most likely to struggle with technical content therefore remains untested.
